the Japs all make as much noise with their soup as possible - a sign with them of

his soup out as hard as the rest had been sucking theirs in. We had
saki, raw fish,
rice, bamboo salad and all the other standard delicasies - all of which Groeger ate

After lunch we drove out to the Airport which is
about
the
same distance from town as most Amerivan ports.
It is a very good one and
will
be much bette r
when completed.
We left Tokyo at nine fifteen that night by sleeper for Kobe where we had
planned to rejoin this boat. We had hot been able to reserve space: and the only
thing left was an upper berth each in separate compartments. The man who had the
lower under me could give the late Clarence Howard cards and spades as a "hocker".
The performance kept up all night, and with the frequent and somewhat rough stops
kept me awake a good part of the night. We got to Kobe in time to catch the boat and
today have had a beautiful trip through the Inland Sea down to Nagasaki. Here we are
spending the night while the ship is taking on coal. The latter operation would de-
light the soul of a "Technocrat"
• Barges of coal are brought along side, ladders are
trung up to the coal holes and the n thousands of men and women pass small baskett
from one to another. This ship holds the Worlds record for coaling, and the record
was made here at Nagasaki. The Japs swarm over the barges like ants and a steady
flow of coal goes into the ship - something like three thousand tons in six hours.
Tomorrow morning we are going ashore for a little while to look around,
and then at ten oclock we sail for Shanghai. Must stop now and get some sleep as it
is quite late and I can hear the man in the stateroom next door getting restless.
